segments.text: Let's start with a common scenario.
You ask three people you trust.
How much should I study for my exam?
Your science teacher looks at the curriculum and says three hours.
Your mom texts a schedule and says 30 minutes because you have to work tonight.
Then your best friend chimes in with studying is overrated.
Each person brings their own lived experience to the question,
and that background directly shapes the advice they give you.
You heard three perspectives.
Imagine an AI learned from only one.
Consider a system that gets all of its study advice exclusively from websites
written by science teachers.
When you ask that system, how much should I study for my exam?
It outputs three hours.
This is a perfect example of training bias in action.
This graphic breaks down two distinct ways this bias occurs.
Looking at the left side, we see a funnel representing data entering the system.
The first mechanism happens when a specific piece of information shows up too often.
During its training process, the AI encounters a massive volume of identical advice.
Because three hours keeps appearing repeatedly across all those teacher sites,
the system learns to prioritize it and makes it the default answer.
When an AI is bombarded with a single perspective,
it uses the frequency of that data as a substitute for universal truth.
Moving to the right side of the graphic, we encounter the inverse problem.
When information gets left out entirely.
An AI cannot account for situations, variables, or perspectives
that were never included in its training examples.
Students who work evening shifts are completely absent from those teacher-authored websites.
As a result, the AI has no reference points for how they prepare for exams,
so its advice overlooks them.
A system's output is limited as much by the data it lacks as it is shaped by the data it possesses.
Let's apply this to a practical example.
Say you ask an AI for examples of successful entrepreneurs,
and it generates a list of ten tech founders.
Looking closely at the screen, you might realize a rigid pattern and ask,
wait, why are all ten in tech?
It is easy to assume the system has a built-in prejudice.
However, the list tells you which industry showed up.
You'd need more evidence to know why.
Before we look at the toolkit, hit pause.
If you wanted to force the AI to look outside the tech industry,
how would you phrase your next prompt?
Spotting an overwhelmingly uniform pattern in the output
is the essential first step before attempting to course correct the system.
This board outlines three actionable strategies you can use
when you suspect training bias in an AI's response.
This board outlines three actionable strategies you can use
when you suspect training bias in an AI's response.
First, you can try to identify omissions directly
by asking what's missing from this answer.
Second, you can challenge the dominant data by prompting
show me examples that don't fit the pattern you just gave.
Third, you can filter out the most frequent data points
by telling the system answer again, leaving out the most famous examples.
These techniques help broaden the scope of the output,
but they have a hard limit.
They cannot magically generate data or perspectives
that were never present in the original training set.
Better prompting is an effective tool for exploring what the AI knows,
but it cannot cure missing foundational data.
This final summary text locks in the core mechanism we've covered today.
AI learns from its training data.
Bias in the data can shape the answer.
Third, you can filter out the answer.
